chapter: Second session: boyhood, brothers and early road years
title: Working for tailors as a delivery boy
summary: Spikes describes cutting accessories and delivering bundles between pantsmakers, vestmakers and coatmakers for several tailors at a dollar and a half to three dollars a week.

story.theme_name: Growing up and learning music: family, first instruments, teachers
story.community_name: Where I came from: parents, siblings and birth

blocks.x: And after you sold newspapers, your next job was...was that when you started Special Delivery, or...or was that later?

After I stopped selling newspapers, I commenced to work in...uh, you know...messenger boy. I had a bicycle, and I get jobs for...in a tailor shop for delivering packages, and when it wasn't delivering packages, they'd give me a job where I'd cut all the linings, you know, for the coats...and buttons. If you was gonna put a grey suit, you'd lay out a dozen grey buttons, you know, whatever

it's gonna be, you know, a three-button suit, you'd lay them out, you'd get 'em up and you put for the sleeves and you put for the vest, and you'd put the whole thing in a package and tie it up and put it in a hole, so when the guy, when he sewed a grey suit or anything, he just reach up and get the package after he drawed the design on the table for the pattern, you know, and you cut that all out, then he wrap it all up and stick that package in there. He didn't have to look for it. If it was a black suit, he'd reach up and get the black package for the black. And that was your job when you was inside. And then I used to have a big sewer in here those great big old shears this big, and you be cuttin' and...but they got used to it, you know.
Well, you were pretty young to be cutting out stuff for tailors, weren't you, I mean...

I didn't cut out stuff--only for the accessories, see? Just pockets. You know, it's the same thing, saying you cut out like this, like that, and that fits all pants. See? You know exactly what to cut--hip pockets and front pockets and the...so many buttons. The vest, and you have six buttons; if it's a coat, three buttons and three buttons on the sleeve. You get all them out the ..... and match them up, see? Then put 'em in a package, and your stiffening material--it's all the same for all coats, all the size, you know. The tailor can cut them to the size he wants. You get 'em...You got a pattern therewill fit...he might have to trim a little here and there or somthing, you know, but they practically all

the same. You lay a pattern down, and you cut it out. That's... that'll fit all suits from, say, 36 to 42, and you get 42 to 48, and that pattern...when he...when the man puts the suit together... the coat together, he'll probably trim it if it's a little too long or a little too big or something. And then, in those days, a lot of tailor shops had a man that made pants on First Street and then a man who made vests on Third Street and maybe a man who made coats up on Broadway there somewhere, and so there were pantsmakers and vestmakers and...uh...coatmakers. If they didn't make it in the shop, they sent it out, and that was what the delivery boy was. See, I carry out maybe four, five of these bundles every day in a good shop, and I deliver them, the pants over here and the coat over there and the vest over here. Then I'd go get 'em for try-on. If the man supposed to come in and try on the suit--it's only basted up, you know, for the try-on--you go pick them up and bring 'em in, and your tailor tries them on and fits them and everything and marks them where they supposed to be cut and where they supposed to be trimmed, the length of the sleeves and that, then you carry them back, and the man finishes the coat. Then you go get it and bring it in, you get the pants over here, the coat over there, the vest over here, and you got the whole suit.
What was the name of the tailor you worked for?
Oh, I worked for four or five of them. Yeah, whenever they'd give me fifty cents more, I'd go, you know. They started you...when I first started, I get about a dollar and a half
a week, and I worked it up. Sometimes I worked it up maybe where I was getting three dollars a week.
You were a pretty good businessman from the beginning.

Well, if this guy over here give you fifty cents more a week, you'd...I'd quit this job and go over there. That...you know, in those days, to get two-and-a-half, three dollars a week is pretty good. That's when I was selling papers. When I was selling papers, I made two or three dollars a week, too.
